title: Adaptive throttle + blackhole + key-rotation: oncall notes and runbook sketch
content:
Status: draft runbook sketch + oncall playbook notes for mixed incidents involving sudden traffic floods, credential/key leakage, and rapid WAF rule churn. These are working notes from a recent paging window (Feb 9 UTC) and a set of proposed quick mitigations and follow-ups.

Summary / high level:
- Problem observed: large anomalous burst of generation requests from multiple API keys, sustained at high RPS for ~18 minutes, triggering token-based quota exhaustion and elevated error rates across inference frontend. Concurrently, telemetry showed many ephemeral client ids with identical prompt patterns (fingerprinting).
- Impact: customer-facing latency spikes (P95 doubled), short-term 502/504 rate as backend queue saturated; internal cost exposure risk due to unbounded tokens consumed by the flood.
- Root cause hypothesis: automated scraping using leaked/stolen keys + horizontally distributed bot cluster; likely partial key exposure from a third-party integration (ongoing investigation).

Detection signals that mattered:
- API gateway rate spikes: sudden 8x baseline sustained for 10+ minutes (see metric: api.gateway.request_count by api_key).
- Early KYV (key-usage-variance) alert: high entropic distribution of user-agent + prompt similarity metric — indicator of scripted clients.
- Token burn chart: per-minute token consumption spiked; billing guardrails would have been hit if allowed to persist.
- WAF: initially had false negatives — rule set did not match the fingerprinting pattern; adding signature rules helped but caused collateral blocks.

Immediate mitigation actions performed (timeline):
- T+0m: Pager to SRE. Oncall engaged and paused non-critical background jobs.
- T+2m: Enabled emergency global token throttle (soft cap at 3x normal burst) via runtime control-plane feature (CLI command below).
  - CLI example: redwoodctl throttle set --scope global --rate 3rps --burst 1000 
- T+4m: Scoped blackhole rule for top 50 offender IPs (temporary network-level drop) in edge ACL while forensic logs were collected.
- T+6m: Rotated three compromised API keys identified by rapid-scan heuristics and isolated owners; issued temporary tokens to impacted customers with explanatory email template.
- T+9m: Deployed narrowed WAF signature targeting repeated prompt headers and UA fingerprint. Reverted two overly-broad rules after monitoring false-positive rate.
- T+18m: Traffic normalized, throttles relaxed gradually after 30m stable window.

Runbook sketch: immediate play actions (ordered checklist for oncall)
1) Validate signal: confirm spike present on api.gateway.* and tokens-per-minute dashboards; check KYV alert and prompt-similarity metric.
2) Turn on emergency-global-throttle (soft cap) to protect backend. Use conservative thresholds then tighten. Record command and parameters in pager thread.
3) Identify top offender keys and IPs (query examples below). Suspend/rotate keys selectively; prefer targeted rotation over global rotations.
4) If attacker is distributed and rotation insufficient, consider targeted blackhole for IP CIDR ranges, combined with WAF signatures.
5) Communicate: post to #sre-incident with short summary, impacted customers list, and temporary ETA. Escalate to product security if key leakage suspected.
6) Collect forensics: dump request traces (headers + prompt hash) for the attack window and upload to secure storage.
7) Observe for collateral: monitor 5xx, latency, and client complaints. Rollback any WAF rules that introduce >1% false positive rate within 10 minutes.
8) Post-incident: open a detailed incident ticket, tag affected customers, propose long-term mitigations.

Helpful queries / quick diagnostics (examples to paste/run):
- Top keys by requests (BigQuery):
  SELECT api_key, COUNT(1) AS reqs, SUM(tokens) AS tokens FROM `telemetry.requests` WHERE timestamp BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 30 MINUTE) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() GROUP BY api_key ORDER BY reqs DESC LIMIT 200;
- Prompt-similarity fingerprint (approx): compute hash of normalized prompt and group; flag groups with >N unique keys.
- KYV check (PromQL): sum(rate(api_gateway_requests_total[1m])) by (api_key) / sum(rate(api_gateway_requests_total[1m])) ignoring (api_key) -> can be adapted to compute variance.
- WAF log pattern: grep by request body signature and UA; correlate with cloud-edge logs.

Key trade-offs and notes:
- Global rotation vs targeted rotation: global rotation stops attack but creates a large customer support burden. Prefer targeted rotation when we can tie activity to a subset of keys.
- Blackhole rules reduce noise but risk blocking legitimate clients behind NATs; prefer IP + UA + prompt hash combos when possible.
- WAF tuning is powerful but brittle: avoid adding broad regexes. Add narrowly-scoped rules, and have a rapid rollback plan.

Post-incident follow-ups (owners proposed):
- expand KYV alerting to include prompt-hash clustering: owner Marco Alvarez, ticket SRE-4321.
- build 'one-click key-rotation' customer flow for managed rotations: owner Liam Chen, infra PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/786.
- add temporary-token telemetry to show post-rotation usage and detect replays: owner Priya Shah.
- formalize WAF rule review cadence and a canary testing job: owner Aisha Moreno.

Open questions / research items:
- Are we able to reliably de-anonymize distributed bot clusters that use rotating proxies? What telemetry helps (TLS JA3, UA fingerprinting, request timing patterns)?
- Should we expose a self-service key-revoke endpoint for customers (rate-limited) to help them immediately handle suspected leaks?
- How to quantify acceptable cost-exposure risk before auto-cutoff (tolerable $ amount)? Put this into an oncall spending guard.

Communications templates (to reuse):
- Short customer-facing email for key rotation:
  Subject: Temporary API key rotation for safety
  Body: We detected suspicious activity on your API key and rotated it as a precaution. A new key has been provisioned in your console with a temporary TTL. Please review usage and rotate secrets on your side. Contact support if you need help.

Next steps to finalize runbook (actionable items):
- convert this doc into a formal runbook with play buttons wired to 'redwoodctl' endpoints (owner: Liam)
- create a test harness to simulate key-leak bursts and validate throttles + blackhole rules without impacting production (owner: Marco)
- schedule a blameless postmortem with product-security, customer-success, and infra (owner: Priya)

Notes to self / oncall tips:
- avoid immediate broad WAF regex sweeps. Start narrow, monitor FP rate for 10m, then widen cautiously.
- always capture the first 10K requests raw headers if storage is permitted; they are gold for attribution.
- keep canned email templates in the incident repo for faster comms.

End of sketch. This doc is intentionally rough — meant for SREs to iterate. Add concrete CLI snippets, dashboard links, and runbook automation hooks here as we convert to a final playbook.
